'''Elizabeth Amy Kreiser Weisburger''' (April 9, 1924 – February 12, 2019) was an American [[chemist]] who made significant contributions in medicine and chemistry, specifically chemical [[carcinogenesis]].<ref name="Elizabeth Weisburger">{{cite news |title=Elizabeth Weisburger |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/washingtonpost/obituary.aspx?n=elizabeth-weisburger&pid=191799135 |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |access-date=25 August 2020}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Mahon |first1=Melissa |last2=Roscher |first2=Nina Matheny |date=1998 |title=Elizabeth Weisburger: More Than a Chemist |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24531163 |journal=Journal of the Washington Academy of Sciences |volume=85 |issue=3 |pages=235–239 |jstor=24531163 |issn=0043-0439}}</ref> She worked for nearly 40 years at the [[National Cancer Institute]] and received multiple awards for her work.<ref name=":2" />  Weisburger's research in chemical carcinogenesis was necessary in order to find treatments for cancer. Some of Weisburger's work included studying carcinogenesis, looking at the activity of carcinogens, and determining the dangers of chemotherapy drugs. Elizabeth Weisburger is considered a pioneer in chemical carcinogenesis.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Women in Chemistry and Physics: A Bibliographic Sourcebook|last1=Grinstein|first1=Louise|last2=Rose|first2=Rose|author-link3=Miriam Rafailovich|last3=Rafailovich|first3=Miriam|publisher=Greenwood Press|year=1993|pages=581–585}}</ref><ref name=":3" />

== Biography ==
Elizabeth Amy Kreiser Weisburger was born on April 9, 1924, in [[Finland, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" />  She was one of 10 children.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://preventcancer.aicr.org/site/News2?page=NewsArticle&id=7579&news_iv_ctrl=0&abbr=res_|title=Scientist in the Spotlight: Dr. Elizabeth Weisburger|date=2004|website=American Institute for Cancer Research}}</ref>  At a very young age her family moved to [[Ono, Pennsylvania]], were Elizabeth grew up. Both of her parents were teachers along with many of her relatives so Elizabeth began learning at a young age at home. In 1944, she received a B.S. degree in chemistry from [[Lebanon Valley College]] in Annville, Pennsylvania. Elizabeth accepted a graduate assistantship job at the University of Cincinnati. In 1947, she received a Ph.D. degree from the [[University of Cincinnati]].<ref name=":2" /> She continued to work at Cincinnati after receiving her degree. She married John Hans Weisburger in April 1947 who was also a graduate student at the University of Cincinnati.<ref name=":1" /> In 1949, John and Elizabeth Weisburger began postdoctoral studies at the [[National Cancer Institute]]. They had three children together<ref name=":3" /> and continued to work together until 1972 when John left the National Cancer Institute. In 1974, John and Elizabeth got divorced.

In 1988, Weisburger retired from the National Cancer Institute.<ref name=":0" /> She had four grandchildren and latterly worked for a consulting company and tutored children.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /> Weisburger died in [[Rockville, Maryland]], in February  2019 at the age of 94.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Linda |title=Obituary: Elizabeth K. Weisburger |journal=Chemical & Engineering News |date=30 May 2019 |volume=97 |issue=22 |url=https://cen.acs.org/people/obituaries/Obituary-Elizabeth-K-Weisburger/97/i22}}</ref>

== Career ==
Elizabeth Amy Kreiser Weisburger's contributions to science are in the field of chemical carcinogenesis particularly on the molecular level. Her contributions aided in finding cancer treatments along with preventions.<ref name=":2" /> Her career began at the University of Cincinnati under Professor Francis Earl Ray. There she researched [[Fluorine compounds|fluorene compounds]] for [[chemotherapeutic agents]] as well as carcinogenic agents. In 1949, John and Elizabeth both began postdoctoral work at the National Cancer Institute under Dr. Harold Morris. His research was in chemical carcinogenesis.  In 1951, Elizabeth became an officer in the Commissioned Corps of the [[United States Public Health Service|U.S. Public Health Service.]]  She then began work in a biochemistry lab at the National Cancer Institute.<ref name=":1" /> In 1961, John and Elizabeth together started the Carcinogen Screening Section of the Experimental Pathology Branch at the National Cancer Institute. In 1974, Elizabeth became chief of the Laboratory of Carcinogen Metabolism. She then moved to the Division of Cancer Etiology and became the assistant director for chemical carcinogenesis in 1981. After retiring in 1988 from the National Cancer Institute, she began consulting in [[toxicology]] and chemical carcinogenesis.<ref name=":0" />
